The landscape
How OCR works (the general pipeline)
Image
Text
1 · DETECT
Text detection
DB segmentation finds a four-point box around each text region.
→ text boxes
2 · RECTIFY
Box rectification
A geometric transform flattens each box into a horizontal crop.
→ straight crops
3 · ORIENT
Direction classifier
A small classifier flips crops that came out upside down.
→ upright crops
4 · RECOGNISE
Text recognition
CRNN + CTC reads each crop into a sequence of characters.
→ characters

WHERE THIS PROJECT PLUGS IN
Stage 4 only: cropped lines in, characters out. Steps 1–3 stay fixed, so detection errors never enter the comparison.
“Recognition is more challenging than detection.”
Self-supervised learning
Labels are expensive: every training line needs a human transcription. Self-supervised learning (SSL) makes the training signal from the data itself, the way GPT learns by predicting the next word.

The problem
02 · PROBLEM
Problem statement
Self-supervised learning requires choosing which input variations a representation should discard, yet this choice is made by hand and retuned for every new domain. We ask whether it can be derived instead.
For handwriting, reconstruction pretraining now beats contrastive and joint-embedding methods, so the choice moves from an augmentation list to the corruptions a masked or denoising autoencoder must see through. Text images are an ideal testbed: the variation to discard (degradation, medium, script, capture) is severe, structured and often physically modellable, while labels are scarcest where it is worst.
We model the main damage types physically, fit their parameters to measured statistics of real historical lines, then investigate which derived invariances transfer to unseen conditions, and what governs the match between trained invariance and encountered variation.
“Chosen by hand” ≠ annotation. Pretraining uses no labels; only the corruption recipe is hand-chosen today.

02 · PROBLEM
What’s the point of doing this?
Not “another OCR model”, but an answer to: what should a text recogniser learn to ignore, and can we measure that before deployment?
PRACTICAL
Read a new damaged collection with a small model and very few transcribed lines.
  • Archives meet new ink, paper, damage and scanners with every collection
  • Labels are scarcest exactly where damage is worst
  • Gives a recipe: physics-based damage models, fitted to real documents
SCIENTIFIC
Turn a hand-tuned choice into a measured, testable one.
  • Every SSL method decides what to ignore; for text there is no procedure
  • Explains when ignoring damage helps and when it erases the letters
  • Gives a test set of real lines tagged by damage, and an analysis tool

02 · PROBLEM
Falsifiable hypotheses
H1
Derived beats both baselines
Lower error on real historical lines at the smallest label budget.
Wrong if: the gap is within seed noise.
H2
Transfer shrinks with distance
New damage > new medium > new script.
Wrong if: scripts transfer best.
H4
Control
VICReg trained on the same damage loses to our reconstruction model.
Wrong if: VICReg matches or wins.
H3
The sign flip
Invariance should help for damage that leaves the strokes alone, and hurt for damage to the strokes themselves.
Background damage
(bleed-through, stains, blur)
error rise
help
more invariance →

(ink loss, merged strokes, diacritics)
error rise
hurt
more invariance →
Wrong if: one trend holds for all damage types, or there is no trend at all.

Augmentations chosen to “best fit the nature of the data”.
Baloun et al.
IJDAR
Augmentations still compared by trial.
LoGo-HTR
WACV
Contrastive SSL, 10M word images; no damage modelling.
Garrido-Munoz & Calvo-Zaragoza
arXiv · Sept
Pixel reconstruction beats contrastive and JEPA on six HTR benchmarks.
THE GAP
Nobody has derived the corruption recipe from physical models fitted to real damaged documents, or measured whether trained invariance matches the damage met at test time, for text.

OUR CONTRIBUTION
Corruptions derived from physical models fitted to real damaged documents, tested on held-out damage, media and scripts, with a test of whether trained invariance predicts the error.
WHAT IS NOT NEW
SSL for text, degradation augmentation, damage simulators. We build on them; the full comparison is in backup.

FIXED FROM THE START
  • the research questions and hypotheses
  • held-out tests on real damaged lines
  • strong baselines, incl. supervised transfer
  • reporting protocol (image height, charset)
DECIDED BY EVIDENCE, LOOP BY LOOP
  • which damage types to model, and how
  • backbone and model size
  • masking ratio and corruption strength
  • label budgets and test conditions
04 · APPROACH
Experiments and data
WHAT WE COMPARE
  • supervised only
  • plain masked reconstruction
  • + hand-chosen corruptions
  • + derived corruptions
  • VICReg on derived (control)
  • supervised transfer
  • off-the-shelf OCR / VLM (reference)
WHERE WE TEST
  • clean modern handwriting
  • same, with a held-out damage type
  • real damaged lines, tagged by damage
  • scene text (camera capture)
  • an unseen script (Indic / Arabic)
Metrics: character error rate, invariance scores, their correlation.
DATA WE USE
  • IAM (clean handwriting, ≈10k lines)
  • CATMuS Medieval (≈195k real historical lines)
  • HTR-United (more historical sets)
  • IIIT-Indic / Muharaf (unseen scripts)
  • scene-text sets (camera capture)
Same backbone and fine-tuning for every model: only what the model was trained to ignore changes. The one new data task: tag a few hundred real lines by type of damage (not their text).
04 · APPROACH
Scope and feasibility
IN SCOPE
  • recognition of cropped text lines
  • small encoders; pretraining is what we change
  • 3–5 damage types with physical models
  • modern + historical lines, one unseen script or medium
OUT OF SCOPE (FOR NOW)
  • detection / line segmentation (keeps reading errors clean; a follow-up)
  • large VLMs as the object of study
  • many languages at once
